question: Is an insured bound by a "full and final" discharge voucher it signed when the insurer refused to release even the admitted amount without it?
facts: After a fire, the insurer's surveyor assessed the loss at far less than the insured's claim. The insurer said it would pay the assessed amount only if the insured first signed an undated voucher accepting it in full and final settlement. Short of funds, the insured signed, received the money and immediately protested that it had signed under coercion. It now seeks arbitration of the balance under the policy's arbitration clause.
gold_issues: Does a discharge voucher obtained by withholding admitted dues amount to coercion or economic duress that vitiates the settlement?
Can the insured still refer the balance claim to arbitration after signing the voucher?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Boghara Polyfab Pvt. Ltd.
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: A claim for arbitration cannot be rejected merely because a discharge voucher was signed if the claimant disputes its validity, for example as obtained by coercion.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Dicitex Furnishing Ltd.
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Withholding payments due can amount to economic coercion that makes a party sign a discharge; the court need only be prima facie satisfied about the plea before referring the dispute.

key_points: Consent obtained by coercion is not free (s. 14); the agreement is voidable at the option of the coerced party (s. 19).
Indian courts recognise economic duress, e.g. withholding admitted dues to extract a full and final discharge.
A disputed discharge voucher does not by itself extinguish the arbitrable dispute.
The plea must be credible and is decided on evidence in the arbitration.
notes: The statutory definition of coercion (s. 15) is narrow (acts forbidden by the Penal Code, unlawful detention of property); the cases rely on the broader idea of economic duress. A good answer should notice that tension.

question: Is a mortgage executed in favour of a 15-year-old mortgagee, who was not represented by a guardian, a valid contract that can be enforced?
facts: A landholder executed and registered a usufructuary mortgage of his land in favour of a girl aged 15. No natural or court-appointed guardian acted for her. Years later a tenant in possession claimed statutory rights, and the girl's successors relied on the mortgage. The question arose whether the mortgage was valid.
gold_issues: Is an agreement to which a minor is a party a contract, given s. 11 of the Contract Act?
Does it matter that the transaction benefits the minor?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Mathai Mathai v. Joseph Mary
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Competence to contract is a condition of a valid contract; a mortgage in the name of a minor not represented by a guardian is void ab initio even if it is in her interest (applying Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose).

key_points: Section 11 requires parties to be of the age of majority; a minor's agreement is void (Mohori Bibee).
The Court held the mortgage void although it favoured the minor, because she was not represented by a guardian.
A good answer notes the older view that a minor may be a beneficiary or promisee of a completed transfer, and why the Court did not follow it here.
notes: Reviewer: the holding treats a mortgage in favour of (not by) a minor as void; check that the item states it no wider than the judgment does. Mohori Bibee is Privy Council and not in the corpus, so it is not a gold authority.

question: Can a partner recover his share of losses from a partnership formed to enter into wagering transactions?
facts: Two traders agreed to share profits and losses of forward contracts in grain that both knew would be settled only by paying differences, never by delivery. The contracts made a loss, which one partner paid to the counterparties. He sued the other for half. The defendant argued that the partnership was itself unlawful because its object was wagering.
gold_issues: Are wagering agreements void or illegal under the Contract Act?
Is an agreement collateral to a wager (a partnership to carry on wagers) unlawful under s. 23?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Gherulal Parakh v. Mahadeodas Maiya
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: A wagering contract is void under s. 30 but not forbidden by law, so an agreement collateral to it, such as a partnership to carry on wagering transactions, is not unlawful under s. 23.

key_points: Section 30 makes wagers void (unenforceable), not illegal.
Void is not the same as forbidden by law; collateral agreements survive unless another law forbids them.
Public policy under s. 23 is not extended to new heads merely because wagering is disapproved.
The partner can recover the share of the losses.
notes: Reviewer: not confirmed from the corpus text; check whether any State law would treat wagers or collateral agreements differently on these facts, and add it if so.

question: How are damages measured when a seller fails to deliver goods, and can the buyer claim his lost profit at a distant market?
facts: A seller at Kanpur agreed to supply canvas to a buyer, who intended to resell it in Calcutta. The seller failed to deliver. The buyer did not buy substitute canvas and sued for the profit he would have made at Calcutta prices. He led no evidence of the Kanpur market price on the date of breach.
gold_issues: What is the measure of damages for non-delivery of goods under s. 73?
Does the buyer's duty to mitigate limit what he can recover?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Murlidhar Chiranjilal v. Harishchandra Dwarkadas
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: The injured party is to be put in the position as if the contract had been performed, but must take reasonable steps to mitigate; for non-delivery the measure is the difference between the contract price and the market price at the place of delivery on the date of breach.

key_points: Damages under s. 73 cover loss arising naturally in the usual course, or contemplated by both parties.
The Explanation to s. 73 requires the means of remedying the inconvenience to be taken into account (mitigation).
Market price at the place of delivery on the date of breach sets the measure.
Without proof of that market price the buyer recovers nothing beyond nominal damages.

question: Can a seller forfeit the earnest money when the purchaser fails to pay the balance by the agreed date, without proving any loss?
facts: Under an agreement to sell a house the purchaser paid an amount described as earnest money, and the agreement said it would be forfeited if the purchaser did not pay the balance before a fixed date. The purchaser defaulted. He sued for refund, arguing that forfeiture was a penalty under s. 74 and that the seller had suffered no loss.
gold_issues: Is forfeiture of a reasonable amount of earnest money subject to s. 74?
What must the agreement say for earnest money to be forfeitable?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Maula Bux v. Union of India
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Earnest money is a deposit evidencing the intention to buy; forfeiture of a reasonable amount of earnest money under a contract of sale does not fall within s. 74.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Satish Batra v. Sudhir Rawal
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Whether the seller can retain earnest money depends on the terms of the agreement; if they are clear that it is earnest money forfeitable on the purchaser's default, it can be forfeited.

gold_contrary_authorities.title: Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi Development Authority
gold_contrary_authorities.proposition: Forfeiture of earnest money without breach, or without any loss to the seller, can be arbitrary and is subject to s. 74.

key_points: Earnest money is a guarantee of performance, distinct from part payment of the price.
Forfeiture of a reasonable amount on the purchaser's default is allowed (Maula Bux, Satish Batra).
A large amount, or forfeiture without breach or loss, attracts s. 74 (Kailash Nath).
The drafting of the agreement is decisive.

question: Is a purchaser entitled to specific performance if he cannot show he was continuously ready and willing to pay the balance price?
facts: A purchaser agreed to buy a house, paid an advance and undertook to pay a further sum to discharge a mortgage before the sale deed. He did not pay it, gave no evidence of funds to pay the balance, and sued for specific performance some years later when prices had risen, alleging that the seller had evaded execution.
gold_issues: What does s. 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act require of a plaintiff seeking specific performance?
How is readiness and willingness proved, and over what period?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: J.P. Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: The plaintiff must prove that he has performed or been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract; this is a condition precedent and the onus is on him.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: N.P. Thirugnanam v. R. Jagan Mohan Rao
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Continuous readiness and willingness from the date of the contract to the hearing is a condition precedent; the court looks at the plaintiff's conduct before and after the suit.

key_points: Readiness (capacity, including funds) and willingness (conduct) must both be shown.
They must be continuous, from the agreement to the decree.
Failure to pay agreed interim amounts is evidence against readiness.
The suit should fail; the purchaser may recover his advance.
notes: The 2018 amendment to the Specific Relief Act made specific performance the rule rather than discretionary, but s. 16(c) (readiness and willingness) remains.

question: Should specific performance be granted to a purchaser who sued within limitation but two and a half years after the agreed time, while land prices rose sharply?
facts: A buyer paid a small earnest amount under an agreement to buy urban land, with six months to pay the balance. He did nothing for about two and a half years while prices in the city rose steeply, then sued for specific performance just within the three-year limitation period.
gold_issues: Is a suit filed within limitation always to be decreed when time was not of the essence?
Is delay combined with a steep rise in prices a ground to refuse specific performance?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Even where time is not of the essence, the contract must be performed within a reasonable time; delay and a steep rise in prices of urban property are relevant to refusing specific performance, although the suit is within limitation.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Saradamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Given inflation and steep price rises, the principle that time is not of the essence must be applied with care, and delay may make relief unfair.

gold_contrary_authorities.title: Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani
gold_contrary_authorities.proposition: The normal presumption is that time is not of the essence in contracts for sale of immovable property.

key_points: Limitation (three years) does not guarantee relief; the court looks at reasonable time.
Delay plus steep price escalation can make specific performance inequitable.
The plaintiff's inaction bears on readiness and willingness.
Discuss the effect of the 2018 amendment, which removed the old discretion in s. 20.
notes: Vidyanadam applied the discretion under the unamended s. 20 of the Specific Relief Act; after the 2018 amendment an answer must address whether the reasoning survives.

question: Can flat purchasers still enforce the original agreement to deliver a flat after the builder signed a new agreement to pay them money instead?
facts: Purchasers agreed in 1987 to buy a flat to be built. The builder failed to deliver and in 1991 signed a fresh agreement to pay them a sum as compensation for the flat by a set date, which also said the earlier agreement would stand unaffected. The builder did not pay. The purchasers claimed the flat under the 1987 agreement; the builder said the 1987 agreement had been replaced.
gold_issues: What is required for novation under s. 62 of the Contract Act?
Did the 1991 agreement substitute the 1987 agreement?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Lata Construction v. Rameshchandra Ramniklal Shah
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Novation under s. 62 requires complete substitution of a new contract for the old; only then need the original contract not be performed.

key_points: Novation needs a new contract replacing the old one entirely, by agreement.
A new agreement that keeps the old one alive is not a novation.
A new promise that is itself broken does not discharge the original obligation.
The purchasers can enforce the original agreement.

question: Where is a contract made when the offer is spoken over a long-distance telephone call from one city and accepted by the other party speaking in another city?
facts: A buyer in Ahmedabad telephoned a seller in Khamgaon and offered to buy cottonseed cake; the seller accepted on the same call. The buyer later sued for breach in the Ahmedabad court, which had jurisdiction only if the contract was made there.
gold_issues: When is a contract concluded where acceptance is communicated by telephone?
Does the postal rule on acceptance apply to telephone contracts?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Bhagwandas Goverdhandas Kedia v. Girdharilal Parshottamdas & Co.
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: The postal rule does not apply to telephone; a contract by telephone is complete only when acceptance is intimated to the offeror, so it is made where the acceptance is heard.

key_points: Under s. 4, communication of acceptance is complete against the proposer when put in course of transmission (postal rule).
Instantaneous communication like telephone follows the ordinary rule that acceptance must reach the offeror.
The contract was made at Ahmedabad, so the court there has jurisdiction.
The judgment was by majority; the dissent read s. 4 literally.

question: Can the seller forfeit the earnest money when both parties were mistaken about the area of land being sold?
facts: A seller agreed to sell agricultural land, thinking of the area in bighas; the buyer thought he was buying the same number of kanals, a larger area, and the price was reckoned on the area. The agreement said the earnest money would be forfeited if the buyer did not pay the balance. When the mismatch came out the buyer did not pay and asked for his money back; the seller forfeited the earnest money.
gold_issues: Is the agreement void for mutual mistake of fact under s. 20?
Can the forfeiture clause be enforced, or must the earnest money be refunded under s. 65?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Tarsem Singh v. Sukhminder Singh
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: A mutual mistake about the area of land, on which the price depended, is a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, so the agreement is void under s. 20; being discovered to be void, s. 65 requires refund of the earnest money and the forfeiture clause falls with it.

gold_contrary_authorities.title: Kuju Collieries Ltd. v. Jharkhand Mines Ltd.
gold_contrary_authorities.proposition: Section 65 restitution is not available where both parties knew from the start that the agreement was unlawful.

key_points: Under s. 20, a mutual mistake of fact essential to the agreement makes it void.
Area was essential because the price was reckoned on it.
An agreement discovered to be void attracts s. 65, so advantages received must be restored.
The forfeiture clause cannot be enforced under s. 74, as the whole agreement is void.
Distinguish agreements known to be unlawful from the start (Kuju Collieries).
